meta.regime: The geopolitical risk premium is being taken out of the market in an orderly, negotiated way, and that is now the dominant macro force. Iran and Oman have agreed a phased framework for a temporary joint maritime corridor through Hormuz and a joint mine-clearing project; oil has fallen roughly 6% in three sessions and European gas, which was the entire euro inflation story 24 hours ago, has given back most of a week's gains in a single session. Underneath that, the inflation problem is proving domestic rather than energy-driven - Australia's trimmed mean would not fall, Japan's services PPI accelerated to 3.6%, and Boston's Collins says US rates need to rise soon absent progress. That combination - falling energy, sticky core - is hawkish for the commodity currencies that still have a real inflation problem (AUD) and brutal for the one whose only engine was crude (CAD, now also in an active tariff war).
meta.nextBigEvent: US core PCE TODAY at 12:30Z, forecast to ACCELERATE to +0.3% m/m, alongside a Q2 GDP second estimate expected revised lower. It is the last major inflation print before Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's first Jackson Hole keynote on Friday Aug 28 at 14:00Z, into a market where September hike odds sit near 31% - so a hot print plus a hawkish Warsh is the un-priced combination.

dailyRead: Two scores move today and both moves come from the same place: the war premium is being dismantled while core inflation refuses to fall. Start with the Strait. Late Tuesday, Oman's foreign minister Sayyid Badr al-Busaidi met Iran's Abbas Araghchi in Tehran and the two issued a joint statement proposing a PHASED FRAMEWORK for a temporary joint maritime navigation corridor through the Strait of Hormuz, alongside a joint project to clear mines, with technical negotiations continuing toward a permanent corridor and a mechanism for exchanging information, managing traffic and providing navigational and security services. President Trump front-ran the announcement by saying the mines are already clear. Understand what this does to Monday's framing: Bessent's Operation Economic Outcast escalated the FINANCIAL war, but the PHYSICAL war is being negotiated down, and the physical war is the one crude prices. WTI is 80.769, down 1.93% on the day, down 4.29% on the week and now roughly 6% lower across three sessions; Brent is 86.934, down 1.86% and down 5.11% on the week. Yesterday's file said the premium had migrated from oil into gas and that this kept Lagarde's energy channel wide open. That has now reversed hard - EU TTF is 62.34 EUR/MWh and down 6.56% on the DAY, German gas 67.27 and down 2.60%, UK gas 164.13 and down 2.98%, and the weekly gains have been more than halved. So the energy leg comes out of the euro's inflation story and out of the loonie's entire story. Canada is the day's casualty and it is a downgrade, not a warning. CAD goes from 0 to MINUS 1. Two things did it. First, oil: the loonie has had exactly one engine for a month and that engine has now failed twice - it did not fire on the largest sanctions escalation of the war on Monday, and it has fallen 4.29% on the week as the corridor talks progressed. Second, and new, the trade war reopened. Canada's Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne published a 99-page list of retaliatory tariffs covering C$27.6 billion, roughly 19.9 billion US dollars, of American goods at rates of 15%, 25% and 50% across about 700 products - steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, electronics - effective September 8, dollar-for-dollar against Washington's new duties on 20 billion dollars of Canadian goods that took effect Saturday after Prime Minister Carney suspended trade talks. Ottawa paired it with a C$7.5 billion support package, which tells you how much damage they expect. Set that against domestic data that was already bad - retail sales minus 0.8% m/m, composite PMI 49.7 and services 49.1 both contracting, annual GDP minus 0.1% with the quarterly rate 0.0%, house prices minus 2.3% y/y - and the July CPI rebound to 3.0% and the 6.4% two-year-low unemployment rate are no longer enough to hold the score at zero. USD/CAD is 1.38612. Canadian GDP Friday at 12:30Z now lands into a currency that is already marked down. The second change is the opposite sign. Australia's July CPI indicator at 01:30Z beat, and beat on the measure that matters. Headline rose 1.0% month-on-month against 0.8% forecast, reversing a 0.1% decline, with the annual rate easing to 3.5% from 3.8% - but the consensus range was 3.2-3.3% and the median forecast 3.3%, and most of the annual improvement was a mechanical base effect from an outsized July 2025 print dropping out. The trimmed mean rose 0.5% in the month against 0.3% expected, leaving the annual trimmed mean UNCHANGED at 3.6% and above the 3.5% consensus; the weighted median eased to 3.6% from 3.7% but rose 0.4% m/m from 0.3%. The breadth is what matters: market goods and services excluding volatile items rose 1.0% in the month and discretionary spending excluding tobacco jumped 1.5%. That is demand-side pressure across a wide surface, not a fuel distortion, and it is exactly the upside risk the RBA staff had flagged. Read it against Tuesday's minutes, which already showed the Board CONSIDERED raising the cash rate pre-emptively and agreed it stands ready to raise if upside risks crystallise. They have crystallised. The Australian dollar jumped and the September 29 meeting is now live for a fourth hike this year. AUD goes from 0 to PLUS 1 - not higher, because the labour market is still broken, with July employment minus 15,827, unemployment 4.5% at a post-COVID high, participation down to 66.9% and wage growth only 3.2%. But the highest cash rate in the G10 at 4.35% is now attached to a live hike rather than a fading one, and copper has confirmed it, at 6.7567 dollars a pound and up 4.15% on the week and 6.48% on the month. Every Aussie short comes off. GBP/AUD and AUD/JPY and AUD/CHF flip from short to range or long, AUD/NZD flips to long, and AUD/CAD becomes the cleanest cross on the page - long the currency with a live hike against the one with a collapsing oil bid and a tariff war. The dollar is the third thing to watch, and today it is the forward bias rather than the score that changes. USD holds MINUS 2 because the hard data has not moved: payrolls minus 23,000, CPI 3.4% and a five-month low, core 2.5%, Q2 GDP 1.5% annualised, retail sales minus 0.6%, and Tuesday's Conference Board confidence missed at 89.4 against 90.2 with new home sales 0.607 million against 0.620 million and the Richmond composite at plus 4 from plus 5. But the Fed's rhetoric moved decisively hawkish overnight. Boston's Susan Collins said inflation is still too high and has become a pervasive concern for businesses and households, and that should evidence of sustained inflation progress not materialise, it will be appropriate to tighten policy soon. Separately, minutes of the discount-rate meetings show FOUR of the twelve regional Reserve Banks sought an increase in the discount rate ahead of the July 28-29 FOMC, which held 3.50-3.75% on a 9-3 vote. That is a wider hawkish base than the three voting dissents implied. With September hike odds around 31%, the market is not priced for it. Core PCE lands today at 12:30Z forecast to accelerate to plus 0.3% month-on-month, the Q2 GDP second estimate is expected lower, and Warsh delivers his first Jackson Hole keynote Friday at 14:00Z. Carry reduced size on every dollar-leg expression through Friday and treat DXY as a low-conviction short, not a core position. Gold is the interesting survivor. XAU is 4,643.17, down only 0.32% on the day and still up 2.78% on the week and 13.87% on the month, holding almost all of its level even as the geopolitical premium is negotiated away. That tells you the bid is the fiscal one - the July federal deficit was 432.3 billion dollars, the largest monthly shortfall since March 2021 - rather than the war one. But with the war leg going, XAU comes down from HIGH to MEDIUM: the debasement thesis is intact, the geopolitical accelerant is not, and Warsh is a live threat. Silver at 69.155 is up 0.82% today, 3.33% on the week and 18.41% on the month and keeps MEDIUM, helped by copper's industrial leg. Europe holds PLUS 2 and stays the strongest currency, but the case is now purely monetary rather than energy-driven. TE re-verified this morning: deposit facility 2.25% (main refi 2.40%, marginal lending 2.65% - use the depo), July HICP 2.9% with core UP to 2.5%, services 3.3%, energy HICP 10.0%, Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q and +1.0% y/y, August composite PMI 52.1 with manufacturing 52.8 at a four-year high, ZEW 31.4, unemployment 6.3%. The dovish counterweight is unchanged and now slightly stronger, because the gas reversal removes an argument: negotiated wage growth 2.44%, consumer inflation expectations 2.9% and falling a third month, producer prices decelerating to 4.6%, food inflation 0.8%. The July meeting accounts land Thursday at 09:30Z and are the real test of whether TE's model call for a September 10 hike survives. EUR/USD 1.16574, up 0.70% on the week. Japan holds PLUS 1 and got a quiet piece of good news: July services PPI accelerated to 3.6% y/y against 3.2% expected and 3.2% prior - services inflation is the BoJ's stated precondition and it is accelerating. Add July CPI 1.9% with core 1.8% and core-core 1.9%, Tokyo core 1.9%, wage growth 3.4%, real earnings positive a sixth month, unemployment 2.5%, jobs-to-applications 1.18, and Polymarket at 84% for a 25bp move to 1.25% on September 17-18. The tape is still the problem: USD/JPY is 159.380, up 0.18%, and the yen is the only major that did not gain on the week. Keep USD/JPY a HIGH-conviction short with 160 as the defined invalidation, remembering the MoF has already intervened at that line. Tokyo August CPI and July unemployment land Thursday at 23:30Z. Sterling holds PLUS 1 on the 3.75% Bank Rate, the 6-3 vote and the G10's highest gilt near 5.1%, with July CPI 2.9% but core FLAT at 2.6% and services cooled to 3.4%. Note the gas reversal cuts against sterling here: UK gas fell 2.98% today, which weakens the October Ofgem-uplift argument that was the dissenters' best remaining card. Cable 1.36384. New Zealand holds PLUS 1: OCR 2.50% after the July 8 hike, TE's model still forecasting 2.75% on September 2, Q2 CPI 4.1% with core 3.2%, business confidence 56.1 and GDT +2.3% - against unemployment at 5.6%, wage growth 2.1%, a July trade deficit of NZD 1,949 million on a record import bill and two-year inflation expectations down to 2.34%. Treat September 2 as genuinely two-way. Switzerland holds PLUS 1 but the haven leg is now the weakest part of the case: USD/CHF is 0.80360, up 0.15% on the day, and de-escalation is a headwind. What holds the score is the real economy - Q2 GDP +1.5% q/q and the strongest since 2021, a record July trade surplus of CHF 8,141 million, services PMI 63.9, ZEW +10 - against a monetary profile that is pure funding currency: CPI 0.4%, policy rate 0%, unemployment up to 3.0%, reserves rising to CHF 768,260 million with Schlegel's intervention warning live. The instruction for the day: buy the Aussie against the loonie and the dollar, keep the euro long against the loonie, hold the yen short against the dollar, cut gold to a normal position, take crude short rather than flat, and size everything for a core PCE print at 12:30Z.

USD.when: Sept 16-17 FOMC (hold priced at ~69%, but the hawkish base inside the Fed is wider than the market thinks)
USD.note: Policy rate re-verified on TE this morning at 3.75% upper bound (3.50-3.75%), held Jul 29 in a 9-3 vote. TE macro re-verified and unchanged: CPI 3.4% from 3.5% and a five-month low, core 2.5% from 2.6%, Q2 GDP 1.5% annualised with annual growth 2.1%, unemployment 4.1% from 4.2%, non-farm payrolls MINUS 23,000, average hourly earnings +0.1% m/m, job vacancies 7,140k from 7,500k, August composite PMI 56.0, retail sales -0.6% m/m, July federal deficit 432.3 billion dollars. USD holds -2 on that data. What changed overnight is the RHETORIC, and it changed decisively. Boston Fed President Susan Collins said the Fed will need to raise rates soon unless coming data show a continued decline in inflation, calling inflation too high and a pervasive concern for businesses and households, and stating that should evidence of sustained inflation progress not materialise, it will be appropriate to tighten policy soon to deliver price stability in a reasonable time frame. Separately, the discount-rate minutes show FOUR of the twelve regional Reserve Banks requested an increase in the discount rate ahead of the July 28-29 meeting - a broader hawkish constituency than the three voting dissents suggested, even though the FOMC overruled them. Tuesday's data cut the other way and is why the score does not move: Conference Board consumer confidence 89.4 against 90.2 expected, new home sales 0.607 million against 0.620 million, Richmond Fed composite +4 from +5. The week now turns on two events. Core PCE lands TODAY, Wednesday Aug 26 at 12:30Z, forecast to ACCELERATE to 0.3% m/m, paired with a Q2 GDP second estimate expected revised LOWER - hot inflation into slowing growth. Then Friday Aug 28 at 14:00Z Kevin Warsh delivers his first Jackson Hole keynote, expected around 10:00 ET, on financial innovation in payments, with no policy record and remarks he has described as a blank piece of paper. September hike odds are roughly 31%, down from 82% in mid-July, so the hawkish outcome is the UN-PRICED one. Practical consequence: hold USD at -2 but cut DXY to a LOW-MED short and reduce size on every dollar-leg expression through Friday. DXY 99.065, still -0.59% on the week and -2.43% on the month.

EUR.when: Sept 10, 12:15Z (TE model still 2.65% refi by quarter-end - but the gas collapse just removed the strongest supporting argument)
EUR.note: Deposit facility re-verified on TE this morning at 2.25% after the Jun 11 hike, with main refinancing at 2.40% and marginal lending at 2.65%. Use the 2.25% depo, never the 2.40% headline. EUR holds +2 and stays the strongest currency, but the composition of the case changed overnight and traders should know it. Yesterday the euro's hawkish story had two legs: the price data and a European gas market that was ripping. The second leg broke in a single session on the Iran-Oman corridor announcement. EU TTF is 62.34 EUR/MWh and DOWN 6.56% on the day, German gas 67.27 and down 2.60%, UK gas down 2.98%, and while TTF is still +6.88% on the month the weekly gain has been more than halved. Crude fell with it. So what is left is the monetary case, and it is still good: July HICP 2.9% from 2.8% with core UP to 2.5% from 2.4%, services 3.3% from 3.2%, energy HICP 10.0% from 8.5%, national prints hotter still at Germany 2.8%, Spain 3.6%, France 2.1%, Italy 2.9%. Activity is improving: Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q and +1.0% y/y, August composite PMI 52.1 and a nine-month high, manufacturing 52.8 and a four-year high, services 51.7, ZEW 31.4 from 23.4, unemployment stable at 6.3%, employment +0.1% q/q, wage growth 3.4% from 3.1%. TE's model still puts the refi rate at 2.65% by quarter-end, which is the September 10 move. The dovish counterweight is unchanged and now relatively louder: TE's ECB summary leads with the July 23 hold and a more cautious, wait-and-see tone, negotiated wage growth slowed to 2.44% from 2.56%, consumer inflation expectations fell a third month to 2.9%, three-year expectations 2.7%, producer prices decelerated to 4.6% y/y, food inflation 0.8%, retail sales -0.3% m/m. The July meeting accounts on Thursday Aug 27 at 09:30Z are now the decisive test - with the energy argument weakening, a dovish set of accounts is the main threat to +2. Express the euro against the loonie above all (EUR/CAD is now the widest gap on the board at +2 against -1), against the dollar, and no longer against the Aussie. EUR/USD 1.16574, +0.70% on the week and +2.55% on the month.

GBP.when: Sept 17 (Jul 30 = 6-3 hold; the gas reversal just weakened the dissenters' last argument)
GBP.note: Bank Rate re-verified on TE at 3.75%, held Jul 30 but 6-3 with a third member joining the dissent. GBP holds +1, and it is holding on yield rather than on policy: the 10-year gilt near 5.1% is still the G10's highest. Both decisive prints cut dovish once you look past the headline. Labour: wage growth eased to 4.1% including bonuses from 4.4%, employment change +83,000 from +147,000, unemployment held at 4.9% against expectations of 4.8%, claimant count FELL 11,000. Prices: July CPI rose to 2.9% from 2.6%, the first increase since March, but the driver was administered energy on the Ofgem cap - core CPI held FLAT at 2.6% and services inflation COOLED to 3.4% from 3.6%. Activity is decent but decelerating: Q2 GDP +0.4% q/q from +0.6%, annual 1.2%, August composite PMI 52.5. Yesterday's file identified the energy channel as the one thing that could rescue the three dissenters before September 17, because UK gas was +10.90% on the week and pointing at another October uplift. That argument weakened today: UK gas fell 2.98% to 164.13 GBp/thm and UK electricity -0.99%, with the weekly gain cut to 4.55% from 10.90% as the Hormuz corridor framework was announced. Sterling therefore keeps its score but loses its escalation path. There is no UK data on today's slate. Express GBP against the dollar and the loonie - GBP/CAD upgrades on the CAD downgrade - and NOT against the Aussie any more, where the CPI beat has flipped the relative story. Cable 1.36384, +0.78% on the week.

JPY.when: Sept 18 (84% priced on Polymarket; services PPI just accelerated to 3.6%, which is the Bank's own precondition)
JPY.note: Policy rate re-verified on TE this morning at 1.00%, held Jul 31 in an 8-1 vote with Takata dissenting for 1.25%. JPY holds +1 and the fundamental case strengthened again overnight in exactly the place the Bank has said it is watching. July SERVICES producer prices accelerated to +3.6% y/y against 3.2% expected and 3.2% prior - services inflation is the BoJ's stated test for whether the price cycle has become domestic and self-sustaining, and it is accelerating rather than fading. Around it: July national CPI 1.9% from 1.6% and the highest since December 2025, core 1.8% from 1.6%, core-core 1.9% from 1.7%, Tokyo core 1.9% and Tokyo headline 2.0%, services CPI 1.2%, goods 2.7%, food 3.5%, PPI 7.2%, inflation expectations 2.7%. Domestic conditions remain the best in three decades: labour cash earnings +3.4% y/y, real earnings +1.6% and positive a sixth month, unemployment 2.5%, jobs-to-applications 1.18, industrial output +4.9% y/y, machinery orders +16.9% y/y, August Reuters Tankan 18 from 13, manufacturing PMI 55.1, services 52.3, composite 53.4. Polymarket assigns 84% to a 25bp increase to 1.25% at the September 17-18 meeting; Reuters has reported the Bank is considering a faster pace than its current roughly twice a year, and PM Takaichi now supports hikes. The tape remains the uncomfortable part: USD/JPY is 159.380, UP 0.18%, and the yen was the only major not to gain on the week, at -0.15%. The external account still caps the score - import price index at a record 200, import prices +29.1% y/y, terms of trade 81.62, July trade balance MINUS JPY 634bn - though today's crude collapse finally starts to repair it, which is the quiet bullish detail. Keep USD/JPY a HIGH-conviction short and treat 160 as the defined invalidation, remembering that above 160 the Ministry of Finance has already intervened once, so the MoF and a tightening BoJ sit on the same side. Deputy Governor Himino speaks before the decision and Ueda is expected to brief after a G20 gathering. Tokyo August CPI and July unemployment land Thursday Aug 27 at 23:30Z.

AUD.when: Sept 29, 04:30Z (UPGRADED - the July CPI beat on the trimmed mean makes a fourth 2026 hike live)
AUD.note: Cash rate re-verified on TE at 4.35%, held unanimously on Aug 11 - the G10's highest. AUD is UPGRADED from 0 to +1 today on the July CPI indicator released at 01:30Z, and the reason is the core measure rather than the headline. Headline CPI rose 1.0% month-on-month against 0.8% forecast, reversing a 0.1% decline, and the annual rate eased to 3.5% from 3.8% - but the major banks' consensus range was 3.2-3.3% with a median of 3.3%, and most of the annual improvement was a mechanical base effect as an outsized July 2025 print dropped out. The RBA's preferred trimmed mean rose 0.5% in the month against 0.3% expected, leaving the annual trimmed mean UNCHANGED at 3.6% and above the 3.5% consensus; the weighted median eased to 3.6% from 3.7% but accelerated to +0.4% m/m from +0.3%. The breadth is the point: market goods and services excluding volatile items rose 1.0% in the month and discretionary spending excluding tobacco jumped 1.5%, so this is demand-side pressure across a wide surface, not a fuel distortion. It confirms the upside risk the RBA staff had flagged. geopolitics: The physical war is being negotiated down even as the financial war escalates, and for FX the physical track is the one that sets prices. Late Tuesday, Oman's Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr bin Hamad al-Busaidi travelled to Tehran and held consultations with Iran's Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi, and the two governments issued a joint statement that goes considerably further than anything since the war began. It proposes a PHASED FRAMEWORK for resuming safe navigation through the Strait of Hormuz built around two concrete steps: the establishment of a TEMPORARY JOINT MARITIME NAVIGATION CORRIDOR through the Strait, and a JOINT PROJECT TO CLEAR MINES from it. Technical negotiations continue with the stated aim of a permanent navigation corridor, future arrangements for managing the Strait, and a mechanism for exchanging information, managing maritime traffic and providing navigational and security services. Both sides affirmed the importance of joint discussions with the other Gulf littoral states and of adhering to international law and the sovereign rights of coastal states. President Trump appeared to front-run the announcement by stating that the mines are already clear. The oil market had been selling heavily for two sessions on speculation that more progress existed than had been announced, and the statement confirmed it. That is the single most important fact on the page today. WTI is 80.769, down 1.93%, down 4.29% on the week and roughly 6% across three sessions; Brent is 86.934, down 1.86% and down 5.11% on the week; Reuters framed it as oil dropping 2% as Iran-Oman talks ease Hormuz fears, with bargain buying limiting the losses. Critically, the premium did not merely rotate this time - it deflated across the whole energy complex. EU TTF is 62.34 EUR/MWh and DOWN 6.56% in a single session, German gas 67.27 and -2.60%, UK gas 164.13 and -2.98%, LNG JKM -0.81%, heating oil -2.50% and -7.07% on the week. Yesterday's file argued the war premium had migrated from crude into gas and that this kept the euro's inflation channel wide open and squeezed German industry; both of those calls are now reversed by the same headline. The FX consequences are direct and asymmetric. The Canadian dollar is the biggest loser because crude was its only engine, and it is compounded by a separate and unrelated shock - Ottawa's C$27.6 billion retaliatory tariff package against Washington from September 8 - which is why CAD is downgraded to -1 today. The euro keeps +2 but loses the energy leg of its hawkish case, leaving it dependent on Thursday's ECB accounts and the September 1 flash HICP. Sterling loses the October Ofgem re-acceleration path that was its dissenters' best argument. The New Zealand dollar faces its own central bank's stated logic turning against it, since the RBNZ explicitly credited the partial reopening of the Strait with easing price pressure in July. The Swiss franc loses its haven accelerant. GER40 gains a genuine tailwind from cheaper gas and power. And gold is the tell: it fell only 0.32% to 4,643.17 and holds +2.78% on the week, which says the bid that remains is fiscal and monetary rather than geopolitical. Trade it as a negotiated de-escalation on the water layered over an escalating sanctions and tariff regime on paper, with the fat tail still on the physical side: this is a framework and not a signed agreement, Mohsen Rezaei's threat to halt flows if neighbours join the US crackdown has not been withdrawn, and the Iranian parliament's Hormuz transit-fee bill is still advancing.
